content: Human anatomy comprises hierarchical organization levels and interconnected systems functioning cooperatively to maintain life. The body's structural hierarchy progresses from cells (basic functional units) to tissues (cell groups with similar functions), organs (tissue collections performing specific tasks), and organ systems (working together for broader functions). The musculoskeletal system provides structure and movement through 206 bones forming the skeleton, over 600 muscles generating forces via contraction, and connective tissues including cartilage, tendons, and ligaments. The cardiovascular system creates continuous circulation through the heart (a four-chambered pump), blood vessels (arteries carrying oxygenated blood away from the heart, veins returning deoxygenated blood, and capillaries allowing material exchange), and approximately 5 liters of blood carrying oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products. The respiratory system enables gas exchange through airways (nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) leading to approximately 300 million alveoli where oxygen enters the bloodstream and carbon dioxide exits. The digestive system processes nutrients through a 9-meter tract including specialized regions: the mouth begins mechanical and chemical breakdown; the stomach continues digestion with acid and enzymes; the small intestine absorbs nutrients; and the large intestine reclaims water and eliminates waste. The nervous system processes information and coordinates responses through the brain (containing approximately 86 billion neurons), spinal cord (the central communication pathway), and peripheral nerves extending throughout the body. The endocrine system regulates metabolism, growth, and reproduction through hormone-secreting glands including the pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, and gonads. Additional systems include the immune system (defending against pathogens), urinary system (filtering blood and eliminating waste), reproductive system (enabling species continuation), integumentary system (skin providing protective barriers), and lymphatic system (maintaining fluid balance and immune function).

scenario.title: Building Body Systems
scenario.content: Students explore a virtual school building where maintenance systems parallel human anatomical structures and functions. The simulation creates intuitive connections: the building's structural framework represents the skeletal system; electrical systems correspond to neural networks; plumbing parallels circulatory and digestive systems; ventilation mirrors respiratory function; security systems represent immunological defenses; and maintenance staff embody regulatory mechanisms. Students can navigate seamlessly between building and anatomical views, observing how principle and structures apply in both contexts. The system demonstrates both normal function and common problemsâpipe leaks representing bleeding, electrical shorts paralleling nerve dysfunction, and structural damage illustrating musculoskeletal injuries. Interactive tools allow students to trace substances through interconnected systems, perform virtual dissections, and observe anatomical variations between different body types. Challenge scenarios require students to diagnose system malfunctions, explain interdependencies between systems, and predict how changes in one system affect others, teaching complex anatomical concepts through familiar building maintenance analogies.

hypothesis.description: Students will map human anatomical systems by analyzing their components, functions, and relationships. They will identify structural and functional parallels between body systems and built environments, and explain how multiple physiological systems cooperate to maintain homeostasis.
